lesson_title: The Can That Lies About Its Name
hook_text: A tin can sticks to a magnet. Tin is not magnetic. So what is going on?
clip_script: Grab a magnet and a tray of metal. Steel nail: sticks. Copper wire: nothing. Cooldrink can: nothing. Food tin: sticks. But tin is not magnetic. The can is steel with a skin of tin, and the magnet feels straight through to the steel. Rule: only iron, nickel and cobalt are pulled by a magnet, and steel is mostly iron. Those are ferrous metals. Copper, aluminium, brass and lead are non-ferrous and a magnet ignores them completely. Why? Inside iron are tiny domains that swing round to line up with the magnet, turning the nail into a magnet itself. Copper has none. For the scrap yard that is everything: hang an electromagnet over a mixed pile and only the steel comes up. The copper stays behind, clean and valuable.
visual_style: Whiteboard tray of objects, each flashing stick or no stick; a can peeled to show steel under tin; domains as tiny arrows swinging into line.
mood: Myth-busting and confident, every surprise explained.
pacing: Quick object-by-object test, pause on the can reveal, close on the pile sorting itself.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and test ten metal objects at home, writing each result down.
